title: Introduction to physics
summary: What does physics study, how does it measure, and where is it useful?
cards.0.p: Physics studies matter, energy and how they interact. Just as you did a moment ago, it tries to understand nature through observation, experiment and mathematics.
cards.0.key: Physics is about matter, energy and the interactions between them.
cards.1.p: A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested. From results confirmed again and again by experiments, a law tells you what happens, and a theory explains why.
cards.1.etk.hipotez: Air is what slows the feather down.
cards.1.etk.deney: Let the air back into the tube and drop both again.
cards.1.etk.curut: The hypothesis is dropped or changed. The new hypothesis is tested again.
cards.1.etk.yasa: What happens? In a vacuum every object falls with the same acceleration.
cards.1.etk.teori: Why does it happen? The theory of gravity explains it.
cards.2.p: Physics is split into branches by what each one studies. Mechanics deals with force, balance and motion. Thermodynamics deals with heat and temperature. A single event often belongs to several branches.
cards.2.once.soru: Which branch of physics studies how a refrigerator cools?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Thermodynamics deals with heat and temperature. A refrigerator takes heat from the inside and releases it outside.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: Optics deals with light. A refrigerator's job is to move heat.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Nuclear physics deals with the atomic nucleus. Nothing changes in the nucleus inside a refrigerator.
cards.3.p: Physics is woven into other fields. A doctor relies on it when using X-rays and MRI, and an engineer when designing bridges and aircraft. Chemistry and astronomy are built on physics too.
cards.3.once.soru: An engineer is calculating whether a bridge can carry its load. Which physics topic does she use?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: The weight acting on the bridge and the supporting forces must balance. That is a mechanics problem.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: Refraction belongs to optics and does not affect how strong the bridge is.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Radioactivity is about the nucleus. It has nothing to do with how much a bridge can carry.
cards.4.p: To measure is to compare a quantity with a known unit. The result always has a number and a unit. "3" is incomplete, while "3 meters" is complete. Everyone uses the same system of units, the SI.
cards.4.key: A measurement result is made of a number and a unit.
cards.5.p: The seven base quantities are not derived from any others. They are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol) and luminous intensity (cd).
cards.5.key: The SI has 7 base quantities: length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.
cards.5.etk.soru: Match each base quantity with its SI unit.
cards.6.p: You just met speed. Quantities built from the base quantities are called derived quantities. The unit of area is m², of volume m³, and of density (the mass of one unit of volume) kg/m³.
cards.6.key: Derived units are built from base units. For example, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
cards.7.p: We use prefixes for very large and very small numbers. Kilo (k) means 10³, centi (c) 10⁻², milli (m) 10⁻³ and micro (µ) 10⁻⁶.
cards.7.svg#15: prefix is squared for area, cubed for volume
cards.7.key: For area and volume, square or cube the prefix as well. 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³ and 1 L = 10⁻³ m³.
cards.7.once.soru: 1 cm = 10⁻² m. So how many m³ is 1 cm³?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: All three edges of the cube are 10⁻² m, and 10⁻² × 10⁻² × 10⁻² = 10⁻⁶ m³. For area and volume the prefix is squared or cubed too.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is only the value of 1 cm. For volume, three edges are multiplied.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: 10⁻³ m³ is one liter, which is 1000 cm³.
cards.8.p: Quantities such as mass, time, temperature and energy, where a number and a unit are enough, are called scalars. Force, velocity and displacement (change in position) also need a direction. These are called vector quantities.
cards.8.key: A vector carries a magnitude, a unit and a direction.
cards.8.etk.soru: Is this quantity a scalar or a vector?
cards.8.etk.ogeler.3.2: Energy has no direction. A number and a unit are enough.
cards.8.etk.ogeler.4.2: Speed is only a magnitude. The one with direction is velocity.
cards.8.etk.ogeler.6.2: Velocity is given with its direction: 20 m/s east.
cards.8.etk.ogeler.8.2: Weight is a force, and it points downward.
cards.9.p: No measurement is perfect. The precision of an instrument depends on its smallest division. To reduce error, you read at eye level, repeat the measurement and take the average.
cards.9.once.soru: The ruler has only centimeter marks. The pencil tip is between 4 and 5, very close to 4. What do you write down?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The ruler's smallest division is 1 cm, and you cannot read anything finer than that. Precision depends on the instrument's smallest division.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: This ruler cannot give you hundredths. Those digits would be made up.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: No measurement is exact. Every result carries some uncertainty.
cards.10.p: Physics is a shared effort. Ibn al-Haytham explained vision with light, and Galileo measured motion. Newton studied gravity, Curie radioactivity, and Einstein space and time.
cards.10.svg#15: Each built on those who came before
cards.10.key: Science is not the work of one genius but of people standing on each other's shoulders.
cards.10.once.soru: An old idea said we see because the eye sends out rays to objects. If so, why can't we see anything in a dark room?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: To see, light must travel from the object to the eye. Ibn al-Haytham showed this with experiments in the 11th century.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: If the eye sent out rays, we would see in the dark too. So the light must come from outside.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: When you switch the light on, the objects are still there. Only the light reaching the eye has changed.
cards.11.p: Physics opens many doors. Research, teaching, engineering, medical physics, meteorology and software are some of them. Organizations such as CERN, NASA and ESA work with physicists. Hospitals, energy companies and software firms hire them too.
cards.11.key: Someone who studies physics learns to measure, build models and solve problems.
cards.11.once.soru: What does a meteorologist rely on most when forecasting the weather?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: A meteorologist measures temperature, pressure and wind, then uses physics models to calculate how the weather will change.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The weather changes every day. Memorizing is not enough; you have to measure and calculate.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: A calendar tells you the season. It does not tell you about tomorrow's rain.
cards.12.p:
• Physics studies matter, energy and interactions through observation, experiment and mathematics.
• A theory explains why something happens, and a law tells you what happens.
• A measurement has a number and a unit. The SI has 7 base quantities, and prefixes are powers of 10.
• A scalar has no direction, while a vector needs one.
quiz.0.q: Put each quantity in the right group according to its place in the SI.
quiz.0.e: Mass, time, electric current and temperature are four of the seven base quantities. Speed (m/s), density (kg/m³), force (kg·m/s²) and volume (m³) are derived from base quantities.
quiz.1.q: Match each event with the branch of physics it belongs to most.
quiz.1.e: Heat transfer belongs to thermodynamics and the refraction of light to optics. Motion and force are mechanics, and electric current is electromagnetism.
quiz.2.q: The density of aluminum is 2.7 g/cm³. What is this value in kg/m³?
quiz.2.e: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. So 2.7 · 10⁻³ kg ÷ 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2700 kg/m³.
quiz.3.q: What do we call a broad explanation of why something happens, confirmed again and again by experiments?
quiz.3.e: A theory explains why something happens and is supported by many experiments. A hypothesis is a prediction that has not been tested yet.
quiz.3.y.0: A hypothesis is a prediction that has not been tested yet. The broad explanation confirmed again and again is called a theory.
quiz.3.y.1: Observation means collecting data with your senses or with instruments. It is not a framework that explains why something happens.
quiz.3.y.3: A unit is a standard used for measuring. The confirmed framework that explains events is called a theory.
A:ozet: Try first, learn the name after. Run an experiment, measure, and turn the arrow yourself.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Let's begin with an experiment. A steel ball and a feather are released at the same moment in a tube with the air pumped out.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which one hits the ground first?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In a vacuum every object falls with the same acceleration, whatever its mass. Astronaut David Scott showed this on the Moon in 1971 with a hammer and a feather.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: It feels as if the heavier one should land first. But without air, mass does not make the fall any faster.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Being light does not make the feather fall faster.
A:adimlar.1.metin: In everyday life the feather still falls slowly. Form a hypothesis, a prediction you can test: maybe air makes the difference. To test it, choose Air below.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Choose “Air” below. The experiment replays on its own.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: The ball was barely affected, but the feather slowed down. So air resistance makes the difference. Your hypothesis was confirmed by experiment.
A:adimlar.2.metin: You have rods that are 25 cm long. Line up enough rods to cover the table exactly.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The table is 6 rods long, which is 150 cm (1.5 m). With a 30 cm rod you would have counted 5. So the number depends on the unit. That is why a result is always written with a number and a unit, and everyone uses the same units, the SI units.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The SI has seven base quantities, and every other quantity is built from them. Look at the table.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: Why is speed (m/s) not in this table?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: It is derived from length and time
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Speed is built from length (m) and time (s), and its unit is m/s. Quantities built from base quantities like this are called derived quantities.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Speed can be measured, and a car's speedometer does exactly that. Look at its unit: what is m/s made of?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: Speed is not part of the SI
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Speed is part of the SI and its unit is m/s, but it is not a base quantity. Look at which two base quantities it is built from.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A runner runs 100 meters. Speed is the distance divided by the time. Change the time and make the runner's speed 10 m/s.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: 100 m ÷ 10 s = 10 m/s. So the runner covers 10 m every second. The world's fastest sprinters run 100 meters in just under 10 seconds.
A:adimlar.5.metin: If I say "walk 3 km", you cannot tell where you will end up. The school is northeast of your home. Grab the arrow and turn it.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: Walk 3 km northeast and now it is clear where you end up. Quantities that also need a direction, such as displacement, velocity and force, are called vector quantities.
A:kapanis.0: Physics studies matter, energy and how they interact through observation, experiment and mathematics.
A:kapanis.1: A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested. A law tells you what happens, and a theory explains why.
A:kapanis.2: To measure is to compare a quantity with a known unit. The result always has a number and a unit.
A:kapanis.3: The SI has 7 base quantities. Other quantities, such as speed (m/s), are derived from them.
A:kapanis.4: A scalar has no direction. A vector also needs a direction.
